what: Wyndham Hotels & Resorts franchises hotel brands. It does not own most of the hotels that carry its names — Days Inn, Super 8, Ramada, La Quinta, Travelodge and others — but licenses the brand, the booking system and the loyalty programme to independent owners in exchange for a percentage of room revenue.
customers: Hotel owners, typically small operators and franchisees of economy and midscale properties, and the travellers who book through Wyndham’s brands and loyalty programme.
money: A percentage of room revenue from about 9,000 franchised hotels worldwide.
Fees collected from franchisees to fund marketing and the booking system, largely passed through.
moat: The franchise model means Wyndham collects a share of revenue without owning property, employing hotel staff or carrying renovation costs. Its brands dominate the economy and midscale segments in the United States, where a roadside hotel owner needs a recognised name and a booking channel far more than a luxury property does. The loyalty programme brings bookings the owner could not generate alone.
risks: Revenue has been flat to declining, from $1.6B in 2021 to $1.4B, which for a franchisor means room revenue at its hotels is not growing.
Debt of $2.6B against just $64.0M of cash is substantial leverage for a company of this size.
The economy hotel segment serves price-sensitive travellers and small-business road traffic, both of which weaken early in a downturn.
Franchisees are small operators who struggle to finance renovations, and a tired property damages the brand that Wyndham licenses.
The shares trade at about 28.8 times earnings and 17.3 times EV/EBITDA, which is a full price for a business without growth.
opportunities: The franchise model requires almost no capital: free cash flow of $330.0M on $1.4B of revenue, with no hotels to build or renovate.
Royalty revenue is contractual and tied to room revenue rather than to occupancy decisions Wyndham controls.
Economy hotels benefit when travellers trade down, which makes the segment somewhat counter-cyclical in a mild slowdown.
International expansion, particularly in China and India, adds hotels at little cost to Wyndham.
Eighteen analysts average a $95.67 target, about 22% above the current price.
watch: Net room growth and revenue per available room across the franchised system. A franchisor earns a percentage of someone else’s revenue, so hotel count and room rates are the only two levers.
view: Franchising hotels is a far better business than owning them, and the distinction matters more than most people allow. Wyndham collects a percentage of room revenue from about 9,000 hotels while owning almost none of them, employing almost none of the staff and paying for none of the renovations. That is why $1.4 billion of revenue produces $330 million of free cash flow with essentially no capital expenditure. The asset is the brand and the booking system, not the property.

The segment it dominates is the interesting part. Economy and midscale roadside hotels in America are exactly where a franchise brand is worth most, because an independent motel owner cannot generate bookings or trust on their own, while a luxury hotel largely can. Wyndham’s brands — Super 8, Days Inn, Ramada, La Quinta — are not glamorous, and that is the point: they serve price-sensitive travellers and small-business road traffic who want a recognised name and a predictable room.

The weakness is the franchisee. These are small operators, often single-property owners, who find it hard to finance the renovations a brand requires. A tired property damages the brand Wyndham licenses, and Wyndham’s leverage over its franchisees to force upgrades is limited. That tension shows up in the revenue line, which has gone from $1.6 billion to $1.4 billion — a franchisor with flat revenue is telling you room revenue at its hotels is not growing.

At 28.8 times earnings with $2.6 billion of debt against $64 million of cash, you are paying a premium multiple for a no-growth franchise with real leverage. The model deserves a premium; the growth does not support this one. The counter-cyclical argument — travellers trading down to economy hotels in a slowdown — has some truth to it but is usually overstated, because the same slowdown reduces total travel. Net room growth and revenue per available room are the two numbers that decide this, and both have been going the wrong way.
bull: International room growth in China and India adds hotels at almost no cost, travellers trading down lift economy occupancy, and a capital-free model converts it all to cash.
bear: Room revenue keeps shrinking as franchisees defer renovations, a downturn hits price-sensitive road travel, and $2.6 billion of debt meets a 29 times multiple on no growth.
